label: ass:concave
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:concave}
For every ${\bf x}$, the function $f({\bf x},\cdot)$ is $\mu$-strongly concave, where $0<\mu\le L$. We write $\kappa=L/\mu$.

label: ass:gap
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:gap}
The primal function $\Phi(\cdot)$ is bounded below, and the initial point ${\bf z}_0$ satisfies $\Phi({\bf z}_0)-\inf_{{\bf z}}\Phi({\bf z})\le\Delta$ for some $\Delta>0$.
head: environment

label: def:sosp
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:sosp}
For $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, a point $\hat{\bf x}$ is an $\varepsilon$-first-order stationary point of $\Phi(\cdot)$ if $\lVert \nabla\Phi(\hat{\bf x})\rVert\le\varepsilon$. 
It is an $(\varepsilon,\eta)$-second-order stationary point if, in addition,
$
\nabla^2\Phi(\hat{\bf x})\succeq-\eta{\bf I}_{d_x}.
$

label: lem:tracking
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tracking}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:smooth}--\ref{ass:concave}, let $R,\bar\varepsilon$ satisfy~\eqref{eq:tracking-conditions}. If $\lVert \nabla f_{\bar{{\bf z}}}(\bar{{\bf w}})\rVert\le\bar\varepsilon$, Algorithm~\ref{alg:newton-track} returns an approximate solution $\hat{{\bf w}}={\bf w}_m$ satisfying $\lVert \nabla f_{{\bf z}}(\hat{{\bf w}})\rVert\le\bar\varepsilon$. With $m=\lceil\lVert {\bf z}-\bar{{\bf z}}\rVert/R\rceil$, it uses at most $m T_{\rm N}(\bar\varepsilon)$ Hessian evaluations and $m(T_{\rm N}(\bar\varepsilon)+1)$ gradient evaluations, where $T_{\rm N}(\bar\varepsilon)$ is given by~\eqref{eq:local-newton-horizon}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove by induction that the iterates in Algorithm~\ref{alg:newton-track} satisfy
\[
\lVert \nabla f_{{\boldsymbol\xi}_j}({\bf w}_j)\rVert\le\bar\varepsilon~~~\text{for}~~~ j=0,\ldots,m.
\]
The input condition gives the claim at $j=0$, since ${\bf w}_0=\bar{{\bf w}}$ and ${\boldsymbol\xi}_0=\bar{{\bf z}}$. Suppose the claim holds at $j-1$, where $1\le j\le m$. Since $\lVert {\boldsymbol\xi}_j-{\boldsymbol\xi}_{j-1}\rVert\le R$, Lemma~\ref{lem:warm-start} gives
\[
\lVert {\bf w}_{j-1}-{\bf w}^*({\boldsymbol\xi}_j)\rVert\le\frac{\mu}{12\rho}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:local-newton} and the stopping test in Algorithm~\ref{alg:newton} therefore ensure that the returned iterate ${\bf w}_j$ satisfies
\[
\lVert \nabla f_{{\boldsymbol\xi}_j}({\bf w}_j)\rVert\le\bar\varepsilon.
\]
This completes the induction. Since $\hat{{\bf w}}={\bf w}_m$ and ${\boldsymbol\xi}_m={\bf z}$, we obtain
\[
\lVert \nabla f_{{\bf z}}(\hat{{\bf w}})\rVert
=\lVert \nabla f_{{\boldsymbol\xi}_m}({\bf w}_m)\rVert\le\bar\varepsilon.
\]
Each Newton call uses at most $T_{\rm N}(\bar\varepsilon)$ Hessian evaluations and $T_{\rm N}(\bar\varepsilon)+1$ gradient evaluations. Summing over the $m$ calls proves the stated oracle bounds.

label: lem:carmon
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:carmon}
There exists numerical constants $G,\ell_1,\ell_2>0$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em,itemsep=5pt,parsep=5pt,topsep=6pt]
\item $\bar h_T({\bf 0})-\inf_{{\bf x}}\bar h_T({\bf x})\le12T$.
\item $\lVert \nabla\bar h_T({\bf x})\rVert_\infty\le G$ and $\lVert \nabla^2\bar h_T({\bf x})\rVert\le\ell_1$.
\item $\nabla^2\bar h_T$ is $\ell_2$-Lipschitz.
\item If $|x_j|<1/2$ for all $j\ge i$, then in a neighborhood of ${\bf x}$, the function depends only on coordinates $1,\ldots,i$.
\item If $|x_T|<1$, then $\lVert \nabla\bar h_T({\bf x})\rVert>1$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $Q({\bf x})= \alpha \bar h_T({\bf x}/\sigma)+ (L/4)\lVert {\bf x}\rVert^2$. Then, by Lemma \ref{lem:carmon}(ii), the gradient of function $\alpha \bar h_T(\cdot/\sigma)$ is $c_\varepsilon = \alpha\ell_1/\sigma^2$-Lipschitz continuous. Thus, the matrix $\nabla^2Q(\,\cdot\,)$ lies between $(L/2-c_\varepsilon){\bf I}_T$ and $(L/2 +c_\varepsilon){\bf I}_T$, and the function $Q(\,\cdot\,)$ is strongly convex. Let ${\bf x}({\bf y})$ be the unique solution of $\nabla Q({\bf x})=\beta {\bf y}$. For $\psi({\bf y}) = Q^*(\beta{\bf y})$, the differentiation of the conjugate function yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conjugate-derivatives}
\nabla\psi({\bf y})=\beta {\bf x}({\bf y}),\qquad
\nabla^2\psi({\bf y})=\beta^2\big(\nabla^2Q({\bf x}({\bf y}))\big)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
For $c_\varepsilon \le L/8$, the choice of $\beta^2=\mu(L/2+c_\varepsilon)$ gives
\[
\mu {\bf I}_T\preceq\nabla^2\psi({\bf y})
\preceq\mu\frac{\frac{L}{2}+c_\varepsilon}{\frac{L}{2}-c_\varepsilon}{\bf I}_T
\preceq\frac{5}{3}\mu {\bf I}_T.
\]
The $(L/2-c_\varepsilon)$-strong convexity of the function $Q(\,\cdot\,)$ implies that its gradient is strongly monotone, and thus we have
\[
(\frac{L}{2} - c_\varepsilon) \| {\bf x}({\bf y}) - {\bf x}({\bf y}') \| \le \| \nabla Q({\bf x}({\bf y})) - \nabla Q({\bf x}({\bf y}')) \|.
\]
Equivalently, we have
\[
\| {\bf x}({\bf y}) - {\bf x}({\bf y}') \| \le \frac{\beta}{\frac{L}{2} - c_\varepsilon} \| {\bf y} - {\bf y}' \|.
\]
Then, we can apply the inverse-matrix identity ${\bf A}^{-1} - {\bf B}^{-1} = {\bf A}^{-1} ({\bf B}- {\bf A}) {\bf B}^{-1}$ on
the Hessian matrix $\nabla^2\psi({\bf y})=\beta^2\big(\nabla^2Q({\bf x}({\bf y}))\big)^{-1}$ to obtain that
                                                                        
\begin{align}
\lVert \nabla^2\psi({\bf y})-\nabla^2\psi({\bf y}')\rVert \le\frac{\beta^3\rho_h}{(\frac{L}{2}-c_\varepsilon)^3}\lVert {\bf y}-{\bf y}'\rVert.
    
                                                      
                   
\end{align}

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\operatorname{supp}({\bf y}) \subseteq \{1, \ldots, k\}$, equvalently, for any $j \ge k+1$, we have $y_j = 0$.
From the first-order optimality condition of the conjugate function $\nabla Q({\bf x}({\bf y})) = \beta {\bf y}$, the coordinates of ${\bf x}({\bf y})$ satisfy
\[
x_j({\bf y}) = \frac{2(\beta y_j - \frac{\alpha}{\sigma} \partial_j \bar h_T(\frac{{\bf x}({\bf y})}{\sigma}))}{L}, \qquad |x_j({\bf y})| < \frac{2G\alpha}{L \sigma} \le \frac{\sigma}{2} \quad (\forall j \ge k+1),
\]
where the last inequality uses the condition $ G \alpha \le L\sigma^2/4$.
Let ${\bf x}_{>i} \triangleq (x_{i+1}, x_{i+2}, \ldots, x_T)^\top \in \mathbb R^{T-i}$ denote the subvector comprising coordinates strictly greater than $i$.
According to Lemma \ref{lem:carmon}(iv), in a neighborhood of ${\bf x}({\bf y})$, the function $Q$ decomposes into a function depending only on the first $k+1$ coordinates plus a decoupled quadratic term that is the squared norm of the other coordinates. Specifically, 
\[
Q({\bf x}) = Q_{k+1}({\bf x}_{\le k+1}) + \frac{L}{4} \| {\bf x}_{>k+1} \|^2.
\]
We know from the envelope theorem that ${\bf x}({\bf y})$ is continuous in ${\bf y}$. Thus, for every ${\bf y}'$ sufficiently close to ${\bf y}$, the maximizer ${\bf x}({\bf y}')$ remains in the same neighborhood of ${\bf x}({\bf y})$, where the above decomposition holds. We can explicitly calculate the conjugate maximization over each tail coordinate, which is 
\[
\max_{x_j \in \mathbb R}\left\{\beta y_j'x_j-\frac{L}{4}x_j^2\right\}
=\frac{\beta^2}{L}(y_j')^2
\qquad (j>k+1).
\]
Summing over the tail coordinates therefore yields the local conjugate decomposition
\[
\psi({\bf y}') = \psi_{k+1}({\bf y}'_{\le k+1}) + \frac{\beta^2}{L}\lVert {\bf y}'_{>k+1}\rVert^2.
\]
Differentiating this equation immediately yields the required zero-chain property in Eq. (\ref{eq:oracle-support}).

title: Proof
body_md:
For any deterministic second-order algorithm as per Definition \ref{dfn:so-alg-class}, the $t$-th query point $({\bf x}^{(t)}, {\bf y}^{(t)})$ is a deterministic function of prior oracle replies.
Define $q({\bf y}) \triangleq \psi({\bf y})- \beta^2\lVert {\bf y}\rVert^2/L$ as the second-order zero-chain implied by Lemma \ref{lem:zero-chain}. Then, we can equivalently write our hard instance as
\[
f_{\bf U}({\bf x},{\bf y})=-\frac{L}{4} \lVert {\bf x}\rVert^2+\beta\langle {\bf x},{\bf y}\rangle-\frac{\beta^2}{L} \lVert {\bf y}\rVert^2-q({\bf U}^\top {\bf y}).
\]
All dependence on the unknown rotation is in the function $q(\,\cdot\,)$ in the last term. By Lemma \ref{lem:zero-chain}, when coordinates $i,i+1,\ldots, T$ are zero, both the gradient and Hessians of the function $q$ involve only the previous coordinates $1,\ldots,i$. Therefore, we can construct ${\bf U}$ adversarially as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Given the explored directions ${\bf u}_1, \ldots, {\bf u}_{t-1}$, we select ${\bf u}_t$ orthogonal to ${\bf u}_1, \ldots, {\bf u}_{t-1}$ as well as all query vectors $\{{\bf x}^{(s)}, {\bf y}^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^t$. This is always possible for $t < T$ under the assumed dimension.
    \item We complete the remaining basis vectors ${\bf u}_{t+1}, \ldots, {\bf u}_T$ to maintain orthogonality with all queries up to step $t$.    
\end{enumerate}
Under this construction, the $t$-th query has zero projections onto ${\bf u}_t, {\bf u}_{t+1}, \ldots, {\bf u}_T$, so the second-order oracle response reveals information along ${\bf u}_1, \ldots, {\bf u}_t$ at most. The returned gradients and Hessians are entirely independent of the future vectors ${\bf u}_{t+1}, \dots, {\bf u}_T$, while earlier oracle responses remain unaffected because they rely exclusively on ${\bf u}_1, \ldots, {\bf u}_{t-1}$. We repeat the above procedure, and finally we can guarantee that $\langle {\bf x}^{(T)}, {\bf u}_T \rangle = 0$ by induction.

title: Proof
body_md:
We verify that our hard instance in \eqref{eq:rotated-instance} lies in our function class. First, the Hessian smoothness in Assumption \ref{ass:smooth} holds due to the Hessian Lipschitzness in Lemma \ref{lem:pro-psi} and our parameter setting that
\[
\lVert \nabla^2\psi({\bf y})-\nabla^2\psi({\bf y}')\rVert \le\frac{\beta^3\rho_h}{(\frac{L}{2}-c_\varepsilon)^3}\lVert {\bf y}-{\bf y}'\rVert\ \le\frac{(\frac{5}{8})^{\frac{3}{2}}}{10 \cdot (\frac{3}{8})^3} \lVert {\bf y}-{\bf y}'\rVert <\rho\lVert {\bf y}-{\bf y}'\rVert.
\]
And the gradient smoothness in Assumption \ref{ass:smooth} is also satisfied, because for $\kappa \ge 16$,  we have
\[
\lVert \nabla^2f\rVert
\le \frac{L}{2}+\beta+\frac{5}{3}\mu
\le L\left(\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{8\kappa}}+\frac{5}{3\kappa}\right)
\le L.
\]
Second, the strong concavity Assumption \ref{ass:concave} holds due to the lower curvature lower bound of ${\bf U}^\top {\bf y}$ in Lemma \ref{lem:pro-psi} and the curvature in ${\bf y}_\perp$ is $2\beta^2/L \in[\mu,5\mu/4]$. Third, we examine the final Assumption \ref{ass:gap}. Since $\Phi_{\bf U}({\bf x}) = \alpha \bar h_T({\bf U}^\top{\bf x}/\sigma)$, Lemma \ref{lem:carmon}(i) indicates that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scaled-gap-and-grad}
\Phi_{\bf U}({\bf 0})-\inf_{{\bf x} \in \mathbb R^d} \Phi_{\bf U}({\bf x})\le12T\alpha.
        
                                                          
\end{equation}
Hence, $\Phi_{\bf U}$ has initial gap at most $\Delta$ if we take
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chain-length}
T=
\left \lfloor \frac{\Delta}{12 \alpha}  \right \rfloor = 
\left\lfloor\frac{\Delta\sqrt{\rho_h}}{12\cdot 2^{\frac{3}{2}}\sqrt{\ell_2}\,\varepsilon^{\frac{3}{2}}}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
Since $\alpha/\sigma = 2 \varepsilon$ under the parameter setting in \eqref{eq:scaling}, we can combine Lemma \ref{lem:carmon}(v) and Lemma \ref{lem:resisting} to conclude that
\[
\lVert \nabla\Phi_{\bf U}({\bf x}^{(t)})\rVert
= \frac{\alpha}{\sigma} \lVert {\bf U} \nabla \bar h_T({{\bf U}^\top{\bf x}^{(t)}}/{\sigma})\rVert
= \frac{\alpha}{\sigma} \lVert \nabla \bar h_T({{\bf U}^\top{\bf x}^{(t)}}/{\sigma})\rVert>2\varepsilon.
\]
for any $t <T$. Substitution of $T$ in \eqref{eq:chain-length} proves Theorem~\ref{thm:lower} after choosing the universal constants.
